description: The folder's only genuinely non-numeric file status, and the only one reported by a READ. One record is read and displayed, and the second READ at app/cbl/CBCUS01C.cbl:L93 reports CustomerRepository.PERMANENT_ERROR_STATUS - the two characters '9' and a binary-zero feedback byte - which is the COBOL and VSAM convention for a permanent error rather than an invention: a status whose first byte is '9' carries a binary feedback code in its second byte instead of a decimal digit, and that shape is precisely what the class condition at L162 exists to catch. Z-DISPLAY-IO-STATUS guards its extended branch with two independent predicates, IF IO-STATUS NOT NUMERIC at L162 OR IO-STAT1 = '9' at L163, and every other status in this folder either reaches that branch through the second predicate or does not reach it at all: case10's '92' on the OPEN and case16's '96' on the CLOSE are both all-numeric, so L162 is false for them and only L163 carries them in, while case12's '04', case13's '37', case14's '22' and case15's '23' are all-numeric with a first byte other than '9' and take the L169 ELSE arm instead. A binary-zero second byte is not a digit, so this is the one case of the twenty for which L162 itself is true, and between this case and case10 both arms of the OR are exercised. A translation that collapsed the two predicates into either one alone would pass one of those cases and fail the other, which is the whole reason the pair is written. The call site is the second distinction: case10 renders through the extended branch from 0000-CUSTFILE-OPEN and case16 from 9000-CUSTFILE-CLOSE, and this case renders through it from 1000-CUSTFILE-GET-NEXT - which is why the record pair standing ahead of the failure is substance rather than scenery, since a run that emitted the status line with nothing before it would have shown only that the branch is reachable from an open. The rendered value is derived rather than transcribed, statement by statement in source order. L164 MOVE IO-STAT1 TO IO-STATUS-04(1:1) puts '9' into position one verbatim. L165 MOVE 0 TO TWO-BYTES-BINARY clears both bytes of the PIC 9(4) BINARY declared at L53. L166 MOVE IO-STAT2 TO TWO-BYTES-RIGHT deposits the raw second status byte into the low-order byte through the TWO-BYTES-ALPHA REDEFINES at L54-L56, so with the high byte still zero the field holds exactly that byte's unsigned value. L167 MOVE TWO-BYTES-BINARY TO IO-STATUS-0403 renders it into a PIC 999 receiver as three zero-padded decimal digits. Here the second byte is binary zero: character to hex to decimal to three digits is 0x00, decimal 0, digits 000. The image is therefore 9000 and the line is FILE STATUS IS: NNNN9000 - twenty characters of literal followed immediately by the four-character field, with no space between them. The NNNN is not a placeholder awaiting substitution; it is text inside the COBOL literal at L168 that the original never replaced, and practice B5 keeps it. The charset basis is named rather than assumed (practice B8): ParityHarness.FIXTURE_CHARSET is US-ASCII and the record images below are decoded under it. Because the three digits of a status image are the unsigned value of a byte, they move with the code page whenever that byte is printable - case16's '6' is 0x36, decimal 54, under US-ASCII but 0xF6, decimal 246, under IBM037, and a second byte of 'A' would be 65 against 193 - whereas this case's second byte is binary zero, which is 0x00 in both US-ASCII and IBM037, so this particular image is the one of the two that does not move. That is stated here so a reader who repoints the charset binding can see at once which expectation must be re-derived and which stands. The raw byte itself is never written into this fixture: what is pinned is the rendered line, which is printable US-ASCII throughout and needs no JSON escape. The path to the failure runs through statements that name no status of their own. L94 tests only '00' and L98 only '10', so a status that is neither falls through to L101 MOVE 12 TO APPL-RESULT; the 88 APPL-AOK VALUE 0 test at L104 is then false and the 88 APPL-EOF VALUE 16 test at L107 is false as well - both false at once - which is what routes control to L110-L113 rather than to the L108 MOVE 'Y' TO END-OF-FILE that would have ended the loop quietly. Across the two iterations APPL-AOK is driven true and then false while APPL-EOF stays false throughout, so both states of the one and the false state of the other are covered here (gate G50). The read paragraph's message is the long-form 'ERROR READING CUSTOMER FILE' at L110, where the open paragraph at L129 names the DD instead and the close paragraph at L147 is long-form again; the three wordings disagree in the source and practice B5 keeps them disagreeing. The record appears twice because the program displays it twice - L96 inside the read's '00' arm and then L78 back in the mainline, within one iteration, with no statement between them that could alter the record area - so the two lines are adjacent and byte-identical, and that duplication is preserved rather than tidied away (practice B5). Nothing follows the abend banner: Z-ABEND-PROGRAM displays it at L155, moves 0 into TIMING and 999 into ABCODE, and CALL 'CEE3ABD' at L158 ends the enclave, so PERFORM 9000-CUSTFILE-CLOSE at L83 never runs, the close paragraph's own error text is unreachable on this path, and the mainline's closing banner at L85 is never emitted (gate G35). RETURN-CODE is 12, taken from L101 - a different statement from the L124 that the open-failure cases take the same value from - and one of only the two values this program can produce, the other being the 0 that a normal end leaves untouched at L87. Three fixture rows are seeded and one is delivered, which places the failing read strictly inside the rows rather than at their end: rows 2 and 3 are never reached, so this failure cannot be an exhausted dataset wearing a status, and case15 keeps as its own the one arrangement that sits at the row count. Those same three rows are what case06 seeds, and case06 runs to completion over them, so the two cases differ in the arranged status and in nothing else. The delivered record is fixture row 1 of app/data/ASCII/custdata.txt because a KSDS browse of a file keyed on CUST-ID reports ascending key order and CUST-ID PIC 9(09) occupies the first nine bytes of the image. That image is 500 characters, the width CVCUS01Y declares across its nineteen spans (gate G19), and positions 333 to 500 are the trailing FILLER X(168), present and space-filled, so the line ends in a space and a codec that omitted the FILLER would be 168 bytes short right here (gate G21). CUST-DOB-YYYY-MM-DD sits at positions 309 to 318 holding 1961-06-08, spelt with the hyphens CVCUS01Y gives it and never with the unhyphenated spelling app/cpy/CUSTREC.cpy uses for the statement programs (requirement I1). The unit is the tasklet of customer.CustomerFileReaderJob - unitKind BATCH_JOB - so the two lines already displayed and the non-zero exit are observed together at step level with no JobLauncher and no HTTP in the path (gate G51); a tasklet rather than a chunk step means no commit boundary can disturb that ordering, and the tasklet's own finally is what spools the lines a failing run displayed, exactly as a mainframe spool holds what a job wrote before it abended. No job parameter is declared, because app/jcl/READCUST.jcl:L6 is a bare EXEC PGM=CBCUS01C with no PARM, and no written record is expected, because the program opens CUSTFILE INPUT and issues no WRITE and no REWRITE at all. Statically derived: every expected value here comes from the COBOL source, the CVCUS01Y byte layout, the app/jcl/READCUST.jcl STEP05 contract and the real app/data/ASCII/custdata.txt rows, and none of it was captured from a live COBOL execution, which the eight blockers in AAP 0.7.6 make impossible in this environment; the deviation is recorded there as risk R-A (practice B12).
